To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the class of uncountable languages recognizable by ω- automata is closed under union, intersection, and complementation; (2) the class of languages recognizable by ω-buchi automata is closed only under complementation and the class of languages recognized by ω-co-buchi automata has no such closure property

(1) the class of uncountable classes recognized by ω-automaton is not closed under union or intersection, (2) it is closed under complementation, and (3) it is closed also under Boolean combination if we restrict the class of un- countable classes to those that are definable in a certain logic

the following classes are recognizable by ω- automata and can be learned by our learning paradigms: (1) the class of regular ω-languages; (2) the class of context-free ω-languages; and (3) the class of star-free ω- languages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How can we extend learning theory from finite to infinite structures, and what are the differences between finite and infinite learning?
the following questions:  (1) Which uncountable classes are recognizable by ω- automata?
the following question: What are the uncountable classes of ω-languages recognizable by ω- automata?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a clear difference in the way the two learning paradigms behave.
the class of all ω-automata languages recognizable by ω-regular languages is not learnable in the sense of behaviourally correct, vacillatory or explanatory learning.
the learning of uncountable classes of languages recognizable by ω- automata is not a trivial task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can show that the three mentioned learning paradigms are equivalent and that the class of all languages recognized by ω-automaton can be learned by all of them.
all three learning paradigms coincide for uncountable classes.

we have introduced the notions of explanatory, vacillator and behaviourally correct learners for the setting of uncountable classes and we have shown that these notions are indeed meaningful in that they can be achieved by suitable learners.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for a wide class of uncountable classes, the learner is able to recognize all indices for a given language, and thus the learner can be considered as a generalization of the concept of explanatory learning.
the uncountable setting is not as simple as one might expect, even though it is very similar to the countable case.
the uncountable classes of recognizable languages can be learned under the same conditions that are sufficient for learning countable classes.
